newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Struggling Pharmacia & Upjohn reports drop in profits.
newsitem.headline: Struggling Pharmacia & Upjohn reports drop in profits.

text.p: Troubled U.S.-Swedish drug company Pharmacia & Upjohn reported a surprisingly sharp drop in second-quarter profits Tuesday and said the gloomy trend would continue through the end of the year.

P&U, created by the 1995 merger of Pharmacia of Sweden and U.S. pharmaceutical giant Upjohn, posted a 34 percent fall in net income to $178 million, or 34 cents a share, from $269 million, or 51 cents a share, excluding special items, a year ago.

The results fell below analysts' expectations of 36 cents a share -- forecasts which had already been slashed from as high as 50 cents a share in early July when the company issued the latest in a string of profit warnings.
Second-quarter sales fell 4 percent to $1.7 billion from $1.78 billion, in stark contrast to the surging revenues enjoyed by most P&U competitors.
P&U blamed the poor results on weak sales and the impact of a strong U.S. dollar vs. European currencies, and said the sluggish performance would continue in the second half of 1997.
"It looks as if 1997 is a year lost," said analyst Ingemar Kihlstrom of Aros Securities.
Fred Hassan, the company's new chief executive who is seen as P&U's potential saviour, attempted to put a positive spin on the results, repeating his expectations of a turnaround in 1998.
But analysts were sceptical of the prospects for any real recovery next year, pointing out that the report showed sluggish revenues from P&U's newer, more profitable products.

Sales of anti-glaucoma drug Xalatan rose to $38 million in the second quarter from $29 million in the first quarter, while sales of Camptosar, a drug used to treat colon cancer, fell to $38 million from $41 million.
"Camptosar and Xalatan were supposed to bridge the sales gap but one, Camptosar, has already peaked," said Kihlstrom.
"As sales of older products fall, you must compensate this gap with new drugs," he added.

P&U has pegged its recovery in part on winning regulatory approval for Detrusitol, a drug used to treat incontinence, by the end of the year. If it is unsuccessful in that bid, the rebound could be delayed, Kihlstrom said.
Analysts were also disappointed that sales of P&U's top-selling drug, the growth hormone Genotropin, had not fared better.
Gentropin sales rose to $97 million in the second quarter from $90 million in the first quarter, but fell 2 percent in local currency terms.
P&U's Hassan said a major restructuring announced earlier this month would result in further job losses on top of the 4,100 positions cut since the 1995 merger.
He also said the company would update shareholders in the fall on the progress of the restructuring efforts.
Analysts said costs tied to the 1995 merger with Upjohn continue to weigh on the bottom line.

Compounding its problems is a planned charge against earnings of between 10 and 16 cents a share for the third quarter of 1997 resulting from the merger of P&U's Pharmacia Biotech subsidiary with the life sciences division of British Amersham International Plc.
Some analysts saw this as yet another red flag.

"Biotech only makes up about 5 percent of the total turnover, and it's a very large charge on such a small turnover," Kihlstrom said. "I see it as a warning to everybody to look over their estimates for the rest of the year."
The company's stock price tumbled early Tuesday in Stockholm on the earnings report, but recovered once trading opened on the New York Stock Exchange.
P&U's stock rose 37.5 cents to $38.19 in consolidated midday trading on the NYSE.
